words.definition: Expressed so clearly and simply that it is easily understood.
words.example: Her perspicuous explanation of the tax code left no one in the room confused.
words.mnemonic: per-SPEC-uous — like looking through a clean SPEC(tacle) lens: you see the point perfectly.

words.definition: The quality of being lucid and easy to follow in speech or writing.
words.example: Reviewers praised the manual's perspicuity, saying even beginners could assemble the machine.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'pic' — it paints a clear PICture in words.

words.definition: Letting some light pass through without being fully see-through.
words.example: The bathroom window was translucent, softening the morning light into a milky glow.
words.mnemonic: trans + lucent (Latin lucere, 'to shine') — light shines across but not straight through.

words.definition: The condition of blocking light so that nothing can be seen through.
words.example: The paint's opacity was so high that a single coat hid the dark wall completely.
words.mnemonic: OPA-city — imagine a city so smog-choked that no light gets in.

words.definition: Misty or unclear, so that things are hard to see or remember.
words.example: My memory of that trip is hazy, but I think we drove through three states.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like the heat 'haze' shimmering over a summer road — everything goes blurry.

words.definition: Not stated clearly or precisely, and lacking exact detail.
words.example: His directions were so vague that we circled the neighborhood for an hour.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'plague' — a plague of doubt where nothing is pinned down.

words.definition: The state of having more than one possible meaning or interpretation.
words.example: The contract's ambiguity meant both sides read the same clause in opposite ways.
words.mnemonic: ambi- means 'both' (as in ambidextrous) — both meanings pull at you at once.

words.definition: A person or thing that is very hard to understand or explain.
words.example: Decades after his disappearance, the pilot remains an enigma to investigators.
words.mnemonic: The WWII Enigma machine scrambled messages into an unreadable puzzle.

words.definition: To block or close off a passage so nothing can pass through.
words.example: A clot began to occlude the artery, cutting off blood to the muscle.
words.mnemonic: oc + clude (Latin claudere, 'to close') — like 'exclude,' but it slams a passage shut.

words.definition: To make something indistinct or hard to see clearly.
words.example: Tears began to blur the words on the letter until she could barely read them.
words.mnemonic: Say it fast — 'bl-urr' — the smeared sound of a shaken photograph.

words.definition: Extremely complicated, with many confusing twists and passages.
words.example: Navigating the labyrinthine bureaucracy took months of forms and dead ends.
words.mnemonic: The Labyrinth that trapped the Minotaur — an endless, inescapable maze.

words.definition: Full of many bends, turns, or complicated, roundabout steps.
words.example: The tortuous mountain road doubled back on itself a dozen times before the summit.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'torque' — a twisting force that keeps winding around.

words.definition: Cloudy or muddy from particles that have been stirred up in liquid.
words.example: After the storm the river ran turbid, thick with brown silt and debris.
words.mnemonic: Turbid = disTURBed water — stir the pond and it clouds to mud.

words.definition: To notice or become aware of something through the senses or mind.
words.example: Dogs can perceive sounds far too high for any human ear to catch.
words.mnemonic: per- ('through') + -ceive (Latin capere, 'to seize') — to seize a thing with the mind.

words.definition: The act of noticing or understanding something through the senses or mind.
words.example: Grief can distort your perception, making familiar rooms feel strange and cold.
words.mnemonic: Same '-cept/-ceive' root as 'receive' — it's what the mind takes in.

words.definition: Showing sharp understanding and an ability to see into the heart of things.
words.example: Her penetrating gaze seemed to read every thought I was trying to hide.
words.mnemonic: It pierces through the surface, penetrating right down to what lies beneath.

words.definition: Having a quick, sharp, and eager mind or power of perception.
words.example: A good detective needs a keen eye for the details everyone else overlooks.
words.mnemonic: 'Keen' rhymes with 'seen' — a keen mind has already clearly seen the point.

words.definition: Showing a deep and accurate grasp of a person or situation.
words.example: His insightful remark revealed a truth the rest of us had completely missed.
words.mnemonic: Break it down: 'in + sight' — the gift of seeing INto things.

words.definition: The quality of forming a logical, consistent, and well-connected whole.
words.example: The essay lacked coherence, lurching between ideas with nothing tying them together.
words.mnemonic: 'Co + here' — the parts all stick together HERE as one unit.

words.definition: Easily perceived by the senses or the mind; needing no proof.
words.example: His manifest joy at the news lit up the entire room.
words.mnemonic: 'Mani-' means hand — as plain and obvious as something held in your hand.

words.definition: Plain and clear, so that anyone can see or understand it.
words.example: It was evident from her tears that the goodbye had been painful.
words.mnemonic: 'E-VIDE-nt' hides Latin 'videre', to see — you can SEE it right there.

words.definition: So openly visible or intelligible that it cannot be missed.
words.example: The excuse was a patent lie, and nobody in the room believed a word of it.
words.mnemonic: A 'patent' document lies OPEN to the public — Latin 'patere', to lie open.

words.definition: So intense that it seems able to be touched or physically felt.
words.example: The tension in the courtroom was palpable as the verdict was read aloud.
words.mnemonic: Doctors 'palpate' by touching — this feeling is so strong you could almost touch it.

words.definition: Done or shown openly, with no attempt to conceal it.
words.example: He made no overt threat, but the menace behind his words was unmistakable.
words.mnemonic: 'Overt' is out in the OPEN — the exact opposite of its cousin 'covert'.

words.definition: Standing out so plainly that it draws attention at once.
words.example: In his bright orange suit, he was conspicuous among the sea of gray commuters.
words.mnemonic: 'Con-SPIC-uous' holds Latin 'specere', to look — everyone's eyes are drawn to look.

words.definition: Clearly different or separate, and easily noticed by the senses.
words.example: Each spice added a distinct flavor you could pick out in the finished dish.
words.mnemonic: 'Di-STINCT' — like a sting you feel sharply and separately from everything else.

words.definition: Producing strong, bright, lifelike images in the mind.
words.example: She gave such a vivid description that I could picture every street she named.
words.mnemonic: 'VIV-' comes from Latin 'vivere', to live — so alive it leaps off the page.

words.definition: Giving a clear, detailed picture, often strikingly explicit.
words.example: The witness gave a graphic account of the crash, sparing us no gruesome detail.
words.mnemonic: Think 'graph' or drawing — it paints a full picture in your mind with words.

words.definition: Exact, accurate, and stated with no room for vagueness.
words.example: Follow the precise measurements on the recipe or the cake simply will not rise.
words.mnemonic: 'Pre-CISE' sounds like scissors — a clean, sharp, exact cut every time.

words.definition: To depict or describe something, whether in words or in paint.
words.example: The novel limns village life with the tender care of a portrait painter.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'limb' — an artist outlines each limb to draw a figure; to limn is to sketch.

words.definition: To explain the meaning of something or convey it in another language.
words.example: A local guide helped interpret the ancient carvings for the puzzled tourists.
words.mnemonic: INTER (between) + PRET — a translator stands between two people and presents the meaning to each side.

words.definition: A brief note explaining a difficult word or passage in a text.
words.example: In the margin, a tiny gloss clarified the archaic legal term for readers.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'glossa' (tongue) — a little note that gives a hard word its own tongue to speak clearly.

words.definition: To add explanatory notes or comments to a text or diagram.
words.example: She annotated her worn copy of the novel with sticky notes on every chapter.
words.mnemonic: AN-NOTE-ate — from Latin 'nota'; you literally add a NOTE.

words.definition: A detailed written or spoken account that explains an idea or theory.
words.example: The professor's crisp exposition of the theorem left the whole class nodding.
words.mnemonic: EXPO-sition — like an EXPO where everything is laid out on display and set forth to be understood.

words.definition: A long, formal written work that deals systematically with one subject.
words.example: He spent a decade writing an exhaustive treatise on the ethics of war.
words.mnemonic: TREAT-ise — a scholar TREATS a single subject at ease, page after page after page.

words.definition: A long, elaborate discussion or essay on a particular subject.
words.example: Over dinner the guest launched into a lengthy disquisition on French wine regions.
words.mnemonic: dis-QUISITION — like an in-QUISITION of a topic, questioning it at exhausting length.

words.definition: Kept secret or hidden, not openly acknowledged or shown.
words.example: The agents ran a covert operation that the public never learned about.
words.mnemonic: COVERT — picture something kept under COVER, tucked out of sight.

words.definition: Moving or acting quietly and secretly to avoid being noticed.
words.example: The cat made a stealthy approach toward the unsuspecting sparrow.
words.mnemonic: STEAL-thy — you move like a thief who STEALs past everyone unseen.

words.definition: Expressed with such economy that the meaning becomes unclear; also oval in shape.
words.example: His elliptical replies left the reporters guessing what he actually meant.
words.mnemonic: Think ELLIPSIS (…) — words left out, so little said that the sense goes murky.

words.definition: Impossible to understand fully or measure; too deep to grasp.
words.example: The sheer scale of the universe is unfathomable to the human mind.
words.mnemonic: un-FATHOM-able — a fathom measures water depth; this is too deep to ever measure.

words.definition: Impossible to pass through, enter, or understand.
words.example: The jungle grew so dense it seemed impenetrable to the exhausted explorers.
words.mnemonic: im- (not) + PENETRATE — nothing can pierce or push its way through.

words.definition: Without a clear shape, form, or organization.
words.example: The committee's plans were still amorphous, with no firm structure agreed upon.
words.mnemonic: a- (without) + MORPH (shape) — a blob that refuses to hold any form.

words.definition: Not fixed or known exactly; left uncertain or vague.
words.example: The painting was of indeterminate age, and no expert could date it.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + DETERMINE — nothing has been settled or pinned down.

words.definition: The practice of deliberately keeping facts or ideas from being clear.
words.example: Critics accused the regime of obscurantism for hiding its research from citizens.
words.mnemonic: Rooted in OBSCURE — the deliberate art of keeping people in the dark.

words.definition: Completely sealed so no air can enter; also difficult for outsiders to grasp.
words.example: The antique jar had a hermetic seal that kept its contents perfectly fresh.
words.mnemonic: From Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sealer of magic vessels — airtight and mysterious.

words.definition: Written or printed clearly enough to be read without difficulty.
words.example: Despite the faded ink, the century-old letter was still legible under the lamp.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'legere' (to read) — the same root in 'lecture' and 'legend'; if it's legible, your eyes can read it.

words.definition: Impossible or very hard to read because of messy writing or poor printing.
words.example: The prescription was so illegible that the pharmacist phoned the doctor to confirm the dose.
words.mnemonic: 'il-' (not) glued to 'legible' — picture 'ill' handwriting, so sick and scrawled you can't read it.

words.definition: Clear enough in meaning to be grasped by a listener or reader.
words.example: After a few sips of water, the panicked caller became intelligible and gave her address.
words.mnemonic: Shares its root with 'intelligence' — if it's intelligible, your intelligence can handle it.

words.definition: Impossible to understand or make sense of.
words.example: The announcement over the crackling loudspeakers was completely unintelligible.
words.mnemonic: 'un-' + intelligible — even your intelligence throws up its hands and quits.

words.definition: Giving off or full of bright light; glowing.
words.example: The luminous hands of the watch glowed softly inside the dark tent.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'lumen' = light, as in 'illuminate' and 'luminary'; sounds like 'loomin'' — light looming in the dark.

words.definition: Perfectly clear and transparent, like ice or fine glass.
words.example: The crystalline lake was so clear that swimmers could count the pebbles on its bed.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'crystal' inside it — as clear and see-through as a polished crystal.

words.definition: Having only one possible meaning and leaving no room for doubt.
words.example: The referee's signal was unambiguous: the goal did not count.
words.mnemonic: 'un-' (not) + 'ambi' (two, as in ambidextrous) — not two meanings, just one.

words.definition: Expressed in brief, puzzling sayings that are hard to interpret.
words.example: The coach offered only a gnomic reply: 'The slow horse drinks first.'
words.mnemonic: Picture a garden GNOME muttering tiny cryptic proverbs (Greek 'gnome' = a maxim or judgment).

words.definition: Relating to hidden, mysterious, or supernatural forces beyond ordinary knowledge.
words.example: She kept a shelf of occult books on alchemy, spells, and secret rituals.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'o-cult' — a secret cult meeting in the shadows (Latin 'occulere', to hide).

words.definition: To suggest an idea or feeling beyond a word's literal meaning.
words.example: For many people the word 'home' connotes warmth and safety, not just a building.
words.mnemonic: 'con-' (along with) + 'note' — the extra notes a word carries with it; contrast with 'denote' (the literal fact).

words.definition: Not clearly seen, heard, or defined; blurry or faint.
words.example: Through the fog, the approaching ship was only an indistinct gray shape.
words.mnemonic: 'in-' (not) + 'distinct' — the opposite of sharp, so the edges all blur together.

words.definition: Sounding wise and prophetic, often in a mysterious or hard-to-interpret way.
words.example: The old sailor spoke in oracular tones, hinting that he already knew how the voyage would end.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'oracle' inside it — think of the Oracle at Delphi delivering cryptic prophecies.

description: mid-frequency and academic register — clarity and obscurity
